iroquois.lifeway: farmers (corn, beans, squash) living in longhouses
iroquois.flag: Flag of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy (the Hiawatha wampum belt)
iroquois.text: A confederacy of five, later six, nations (Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca and, from 1722, Tuscarora). One of the most influential political powers of the Northeast, it dominated the fur trade in the 17th century and shattered neighboring nations in the so-called Beaver Wars.
events: Founding of the confederacy (by tradition, by the Great Peacemaker and Hiawatha; the date is disputed).
The Tuscarora are admitted – the Six Nations are formed.
The Sullivan Expedition burns Iroquois towns during the American Revolutionary War.
Treaty of Fort Stanwix; part of the Iroquois move to the Grand River in Ontario.
terr: Homeland in present-day New York State
Six Nations of the Grand River (Ontario)

huron.lifeway: farmers and traders in palisaded villages
huron.text: A confederacy of settled farmers between Lake Huron and Lake Simcoe, and key trading allies of the French. The Iroquois destroyed it in 1649–1650; the survivors scattered – some settled near Quebec City (Wendake), others, as the Wyandot, ended up in Oklahoma by way of Ohio and Kansas.
pop: Wyandotte Nation in the U.S. and Huron-Wendat in Canada
events: Samuel de Champlain visits Huronia.
An Iroquois attack destroys the Huron confederacy.
Settlement at Wendake (Jeune-Lorette) near Quebec City.
The Wyandot obtain land in Indian Territory (Oklahoma).

lenape.flag: Flag of the Delaware Tribe of Indians (Oklahoma)
lenape.text: The original inhabitants of the Delaware River valley, present-day New Jersey, and the New York City area – it was from them that the Dutch “bought” Manhattan. Colonial pressure gradually pushed them through Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, and Kansas all the way to Oklahoma.
pop: all Lenape tribes in the U.S. and Canada
events: Sale of Manhattan to the Dutch.
The “Walking Purchase” – a fraudulent seizure of vast lands in Pennsylvania.
Treaty of Fort Pitt – the first treaty between the United States and a Native nation.
Removal from Kansas to Indian Territory.

wampanoag.text: The nation that received the Mayflower Pilgrims in 1620 and is associated with the first Thanksgiving. After their defeat in the bloody King Philip’s (Metacom’s) War of 1675–1676, only small communities remained of the once large confederation.
pop: estimated survivors after King Philip’s War
events: An epidemic introduced by Europeans kills most of the coastal population.
The sachem Massasoit makes peace with Plymouth Colony.
King Philip’s (Metacom’s) War.
Federal recognition of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe.

mikmaq.countries: Canada (Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Newfoundland), U.S. (Maine)
mikmaq.lifeway: hunters, fishers, and seafarers in canoes
mikmaq.flag: Flag of the Mi'kmaq Grand Council (Santé Mawiómi)
mikmaq.text: The people of Canada’s Maritime provinces (Mi'kma'ki) and among the first to meet European fishermen. They never formally ceded their land; the 18th-century Peace and Friendship Treaties remain the foundation of their rights today.
events: Grand Chief Membertou accepts baptism and an alliance with the French.
The first of the Peace and Friendship Treaties with the British.
The Marshall decision affirms treaty fishing rights.

abenaki.text: An Algonquian nation of northern New England, a member of the Wabanaki Confederacy and an ally of the French against the English colonies. During the wars of the 17th and 18th centuries most withdrew to the mission villages of Odanak and Wôlinak in Quebec.
events: The first of a series of wars with English colonists.
Rogers’ Rangers burn Odanak (St. Francis).

powhatan.lifeway: farmers living in villages of longhouses
powhatan.text: A confederacy of about thirty tribes of Tidewater Virginia under the paramount chief Wahunsenacah, father of Pocahontas. Jamestown was founded on their land in 1607; after three wars with the English the confederacy dissolved, but its descendants still live in Virginia.
pop: estimate based on a count of warriors
rough estimate of members of successor tribes (Pamunkey, Mattaponi, and others)
events: Founding of Jamestown.
Opechancanough’s attack on the colony – the Second Anglo-Powhatan War.
Treaty of Middle Plantation – the tribes become subjects of the Crown and reservations are created.

shawnee.text: A nation of the Ohio River valley, famous for its long resistance to American expansion. In the early 19th century the leader Tecumseh tried to unite the tribes from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico into a single confederacy.
pop: enrolled members of the three Shawnee tribes in Oklahoma
events: Lord Dunmore’s War over Kentucky.
Treaty of Greenville – loss of most of Ohio.
Tecumseh is killed at the Battle of the Thames.
Forced removal from Ohio to Kansas.

miami.lifeway: farmers (known for their white corn) and bison hunters
miami.text: A nation of present-day Indiana and western Ohio. Under Chief Little Turtle it dealt the U.S. Army one of its worst defeats of the Indian Wars in 1791.
pop: enrolled members of the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma
events: Little Turtle defeats General St. Clair’s army.
The confederacy is defeated at Fallen Timbers.
Forced removal from Indiana to Kansas, later to Oklahoma.

ojibwe.countries: Canada (Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan), U.S. (Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, North Dakota)
ojibwe.lifeway: hunters, fishers, and wild-rice gatherers; birchbark canoes
ojibwe.text: One of the most numerous nations north of Mexico, centered on Lakes Superior and Huron. Together with the Odawa and Potawatomi they formed the Council of Three Fires; in the 18th century they pushed the Sioux out of the Minnesota woodlands onto the plains.
pop: U.S. and Canada; estimates range from 300,000 to 360,000
events: By tradition, the migration from the Atlantic to the Great Lakes is completed.
The Dakota are driven from the Mille Lacs area.
The Robinson Treaties in Canada; in the U.S., a series of land cessions and the creation of reservations.
terr: Anishinaabewaki – around Lakes Superior and Huron

potawatomi.countries: U.S. (Oklahoma, Kansas, Michigan, Wisconsin, Indiana), Canada (Ontario)
potawatomi.text: The “Keepers of the Fire” of the Council of Three Fires, settled around the southern tip of Lake Michigan where Chicago now stands. In 1838 they were marched from Indiana to Kansas on the Trail of Death.
events: Treaty of Chicago – cession of the last lands on Lake Michigan.
The Potawatomi Trail of Death from Indiana to Kansas.
Part of the tribe (the Citizen Potawatomi) moves to Oklahoma.

hochunk.text: A Siouan-speaking nation of Wisconsin surrounded by Algonquian neighbors. In the 19th century it was forcibly relocated several times (Iowa, Minnesota, Dakota, Nebraska), but many secretly returned home – which is why there are two tribes today, in Wisconsin and in Nebraska.
events: Jean Nicolet becomes the first European to meet the Ho-Chunk, at Green Bay.
Treaty ceding all land in Wisconsin.
A reservation is created in Nebraska.
terr: Wisconsin – Green Bay and the Wisconsin River

cherokee.lifeway: farmers living in towns with council houses
cherokee.text: The largest of the “Five Civilized Tribes” of the Southeast. Around 1821 Sequoyah created a syllabary for their language and the nation adopted a written constitution; even so, in 1838–1839 it was driven along the Trail of Tears to Oklahoma, and thousands died on the way.
pop: enrolled citizens of the three federally recognized tribes
events: Sequoyah completes the Cherokee syllabary.
The Cherokee Nation adopts a constitution.
The Trail of Tears – a forced march to Oklahoma with about 4,000 deaths.
McGirt v. Oklahoma affirms that the reservations of eastern Oklahoma still exist.

muscogee.text: A confederacy of towns in present-day Georgia and Alabama, heirs of the Mississippian mound-building culture. The Red Stick civil war (1813–1814) ended in defeat by Andrew Jackson and the loss of most of their land; removal to Oklahoma followed in the 1830s.
events: Battle of Horseshoe Bend and the Treaty of Fort Jackson – loss of 23 million acres.
Forced removal to Indian Territory.
McGirt v. Oklahoma concerned the Muscogee reservation itself.

choctaw.flag: Flag of the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma
choctaw.text: A farming nation of present-day Mississippi. In 1831 they were the first to be removed under the Indian Removal Act – one of their leaders described the journey as a “trail of tears and death.” Choctaw code talkers served in World War I.
pop: Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma and other Choctaw tribes
events: Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek – cession of the Mississippi homeland.
The first wave of forced removal to Oklahoma.
The Choctaw send money to help the Irish during the Great Famine.

chickasaw.text: Close relatives of the Choctaw from the north of present-day Mississippi, renowned as undefeated warriors – they repelled de Soto’s expedition and several French campaigns. In 1837 they bought their way into the western part of Choctaw land in Oklahoma.
pop: citizens of the Chickasaw Nation (the Wikipedia infobox gives an older figure of 38,000)
events: Clash with Hernando de Soto’s expedition.
Victory over the French at Ackia.
Removal to Indian Territory.

seminole.lifeway: farmers and herders; open-sided chickee houses in the swamps
seminole.text: A nation that formed in Florida in the 18th century from Creek migrants, remnants of local tribes, and people who had escaped slavery. The three Seminole Wars (1817–1858) were the longest and costliest Indian wars the United States fought; the Florida Seminole never signed a peace treaty.
pop: estimate of those who remained in Florida
Seminole Nation of Oklahoma, Seminole Tribe of Florida, and Miccosukee
events: First Seminole War.
Second Seminole War; the leader Osceola.
Most Seminole are removed to Oklahoma.
End of the third war – a few hundred people remain in the Everglades.

natchez.countries: U.S. (descendants in Oklahoma and South Carolina)
natchez.lifeway: farmers; a society ruled by the “Great Sun”
natchez.flag: The nation ceased to exist as a separate people in 1731 – it had no flag.
natchez.text: The last great chiefdom of the Mississippian culture, with a sacred ruler called the Great Sun and temple mounds. After their uprising against the French in 1729 the Natchez were scattered, sold into slavery, or absorbed by the Chickasaw, Creek, and Cherokee.
events: La Salle visits the Natchez villages.
Uprising – destruction of the French Fort Rosalie.
French retaliation: captives are sold into slavery in Saint-Domingue.

timucua.lifeway: farmers and fishers in about 35 chiefdoms
timucua.flag: The nation died out in the 18th century – it had no flag.
timucua.text: The original inhabitants of northern Florida, the first people encountered by the Spanish and the French Huguenots. Epidemics, the mission system, and slave raids wiped them out within two centuries; the last survivors sailed to Cuba with the Spanish in 1763. Their emptied land was later settled by the Seminole.
events: Ponce de León lands in Florida.
St. Augustine is founded on Timucua land.
The last Timucua leave for Cuba with the Spanish.

caddo.text: A confederacy of farming tribes on the borderlands of present-day Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma. The name Texas comes from the Caddo word táyshaʼ – “friend.”
events: Encounter with de Soto’s expedition.
Cession of their Louisiana lands to the United States.
Expulsion from Texas to Indian Territory.
terr: Borderlands of Texas, Louisiana, and Arkansas

sioux.countries: U.S. (South and North Dakota, Minnesota, Nebraska, Montana), Canada
sioux.lifeway: mounted bison hunters living in tipis
sioux.flag: Flag of the Oglala of the Pine Ridge Reservation – one of the Sioux tribes; the Sioux have no common flag
sioux.text: The great confederacy of the Dakota and Lakota. Originally a woodland people of Minnesota, they moved onto the plains in the 18th century after acquiring horses and became the dominant power there. Sitting Bull, Crazy Horse, and Red Cloud led a resistance that peaked with the victory at the Little Bighorn (1876) and ended with the Wounded Knee Massacre (1890).
events: The Dakota War in Minnesota.
Treaty of Fort Laramie – the Great Sioux Reservation, including the Black Hills.
Battle of the Little Bighorn.
Wounded Knee Massacre.
The U.S. Supreme Court rules the taking of the Black Hills illegal; the Sioux refuse the compensation and demand the land back.
terr: Northern Plains – the Dakotas, Nebraska, Wyoming

cheyenne.flag: Flag of the Northern Cheyenne (the Morning Star)
cheyenne.text: An Algonquian nation that during the 18th century changed from settled farmers on the Sheyenne River into mounted bison hunters. They survived the massacres at Sand Creek (1864) and on the Washita (1868); in 1878–1879 the Northern Cheyenne won a reservation in Montana through their dramatic escape from Oklahoma.
events: Sand Creek Massacre.
They take part in the Battle of the Little Bighorn.
The Northern Cheyenne Exodus from Oklahoma.
The Northern Cheyenne Reservation is established in Montana.

arapaho.text: Close allies of the Cheyenne on the central plains at the foot of the Rocky Mountains. The Northern Arapaho now share the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming with their former enemies the Shoshone; the Southern Arapaho live with the Cheyenne in Oklahoma.
events: The Treaty of Fort Laramie recognizes Arapaho and Cheyenne title to the plains between the Platte and Arkansas rivers.
Sand Creek Massacre.
The Northern Arapaho are placed on the Wind River Reservation.

comanche.lifeway: bison hunters, master riders, and horse breeders
comanche.text: The “Lords of the Southern Plains.” Around 1700 they split from the Shoshone, acquired horses, and created Comanchería – an empire that for a century and a half halted Spanish, Mexican, and Texan expansion. Their last war chief was Quanah Parker.
pop: estimate at the height of their power (P. Hämäläinen); Mooney gives only 7,000
enrolled members of the Comanche Nation
events: First Spanish mention of the Comanche in New Mexico.
The Great Raid, reaching the Gulf of Mexico.
Treaty of Medicine Lodge – a reservation in Oklahoma.
Quanah Parker surrenders at Fort Sill.

kiowa.text: A nation that migrated from the headwaters of the Yellowstone through the Black Hills to the southern plains, where around 1790 it formed a lasting alliance with the Comanche. They recorded their history in painted winter and summer calendars.
events: Peace and alliance with the Comanche.
Treaty of Medicine Lodge.
The Red River War – the end of free life on the plains.

crow.text: A nation of the Yellowstone valley that once split off from the settled Hidatsa. Surrounded by stronger enemies – the Lakota, Cheyenne, and Blackfoot – the Crow chose alliance with the U.S. Army and served as its scouts, including at the Little Bighorn.
events: First treaty of friendship with the United States.
The Treaty of Fort Laramie defines a reservation in Montana.
Crow scouts accompany Custer.

blackfoot.text: A confederacy of the Siksika, Kainai (Blood), and Piikani (Peigan) that controlled the northwestern plains from the Saskatchewan River to the Missouri and long kept fur trappers out. It was broken by the extermination of the bison and the “Starvation Winter” of 1883–1884.
events: A smallpox epidemic kills roughly half the nation.
Lame Bull’s Treaty with the United States.
Treaty 7 with Canada.
The Starvation Winter after the bison disappear.

pawnee.lifeway: farmers in earth lodges with seasonal bison hunts; star lore
pawnee.text: A semi-sedentary nation of the Platte and Loup river valleys in Nebraska, known for its elaborate star mythology. Epidemics and Lakota attacks cut their numbers from ten thousand to a few hundred; the Pawnee Scouts of the U.S. Army were famous.
events: First land cession to the United States.
Massacre Canyon – a Lakota attack on a hunting camp.
Removal from Nebraska to Oklahoma.

osage.text: A powerful nation between the Missouri and Arkansas rivers and the main trading partner of the French at St. Louis. After oil was discovered on their Oklahoma reservation they were among the richest people in the world in the 1920s – and became the victims of a series of murders (“Killers of the Flower Moon”).
events: Treaty of Fort Osage – cession of most of Missouri and Arkansas.
Move to a reservation in Kansas.
Purchase of a new reservation in Oklahoma.
Start of the “Reign of Terror” – murders over oil headrights.
terr: Between the Missouri and the Arkansas

mandan.lifeway: farmers in fortified villages of earth lodges
mandan.text: Settled farmers and traders of the upper Missouri; the Lewis and Clark expedition wintered in their villages. The smallpox epidemic of 1837 nearly wiped the nation out – the survivors joined the Hidatsa and Arikara as the Three Affiliated Tribes.
events: La Vérendrye becomes the first European to visit the Mandan villages.
Lewis and Clark winter at Fort Mandan.
A catastrophic smallpox epidemic.
Garrison Dam floods the fertile bottomlands of the Fort Berthold Reservation.
terr: Upper Missouri (mouths of the Heart and Knife rivers)

assiniboine.text: A nation that split from the Sioux in the 17th century and, allied with the Cree (the “Iron Confederacy”), dominated the fur trade on the northern plains between the Hudson’s Bay Company and the tribes farther west.
events: First mention in the Jesuit Relations.
Smallpox epidemic.
The Fort Peck and Fort Belknap reservations are established in Montana.

cree.lifeway: hunters, fishers, and trappers; bison hunters in the west
cree.text: The most numerous Indigenous nation in Canada, spread across the forest belt from Labrador to the Rocky Mountains. The Cree were the main partners of the Hudson’s Bay Company; some moved onto the plains and became bison hunters. Cree syllabics are still in use today.
events: The Hudson’s Bay Company is founded – the Cree become middlemen in the trade.
The North-West Rebellion; chiefs Poundmaker and Big Bear.
The James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement – the first modern treaty in Canada.
terr: Forests from James Bay to Alberta

navajo.lifeway: sheepherders, weavers, and farmers; hogan dwellings
navajo.text: Today the largest tribal nation in the United States by enrollment, with the largest reservation. Their Athabaskan ancestors arrived in the Southwest from the north roughly 600 years ago; they adopted weaving and farming from the Pueblo peoples and sheep and horses from the Spanish. Navajo code talkers served in World War II.
pop: estimate at the return from internment
enrolled citizens of the Navajo Nation
events: The Long Walk – deportation to Bosque Redondo.
A treaty allows the return home and creates the reservation.
Navajo code talkers join the U.S. Marine Corps.

apache.lifeway: hunters, gatherers, and raiders; wickiup dwellings
apache.text: A group of related Athabaskan nations (Chiricahua, Mescalero, Jicarilla, Western Apache, Lipan). For a quarter of a millennium they resisted the Spanish, Mexicans, and Americans; Geronimo’s surrender in 1886 ended the Indian Wars in the United States.
events: The Bascom Affair – start of the wars with Cochise.
The San Carlos and Fort Apache reservations are established.
Geronimo surrenders; the Chiricahua are deported to Florida.

hopi.lifeway: dry farmers growing corn in the desert; stone pueblos on the mesas
hopi.text: A Pueblo nation of the mesas of northeastern Arizona. The village of Oraibi, continuously inhabited since at least the 12th century, is among the oldest settlements in the United States. The Hopi preserved the katsina ceremonial cycle and never returned to Spanish rule after the revolt of 1680.
events: First encounter with the Spanish (the Coronado expedition).
They take part in the Pueblo Revolt.
The Hopi reservation is created within Navajo country.

zuni.text: A Pueblo nation whose language has no known relatives. Their village of Hawikuh was the first “city” of the fabled Cíbola taken by Coronado in 1540. They have lived in the Zuni River valley continuously for thousands of years.
events: Coronado takes Hawikuh.
The Pueblo Revolt – the Zuni take refuge on the mesa Dowa Yalanne.
The reservation is established.

pueblo.flag: The nineteen pueblos of New Mexico each have their own flag; there is no common one.
pueblo.text: Settled farmers of the Rio Grande valley, descendants of the builders of Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde. In 1680, led by Popé, they rose up and drove the Spanish out of New Mexico for twelve years – the most successful Native uprising in the history of North America.
events: Juan de Oñate founds the Spanish colony of New Mexico.
The Pueblo Revolt.
The Spanish reconquest under Diego de Vargas.

tohono.lifeway: desert farmers and gatherers of saguaro fruit
tohono.text: The people of the Sonoran Desert, heirs of the Hohokam culture. The Gadsden Purchase of 1853 split their land with the U.S.–Mexico border; they still live with a boundary that runs through the middle of their territory.
events: The Jesuit Eusebio Kino founds the first missions.
The Gadsden Purchase divides their land with a border.
The main reservation is established.

yaqui.lifeway: farmers of the Yaqui River valley
yaqui.flag: Flag of the Pascua Yaqui Tribe (Arizona)
yaqui.text: A nation of the Yaqui River valley in Sonora that repelled the first Spanish expedition in 1533 and defended its autonomy in wars with Mexico until 1929. Under the dictatorship of Porfirio Díaz thousands of Yaqui were deported to plantations in Yucatán; refugees founded communities in Arizona.
events: The Yaqui repel the expedition of Diego de Guzmán.
Arrival of the Jesuits and creation of the eight mission towns.
Battle of Mazocoba and mass deportations to Yucatán.
Federal recognition of the Pascua Yaqui Tribe in the United States.

raramuri.lifeway: mountain farmers and herders; long-distance runners
raramuri.text: Highlanders of the Sierra Madre Occidental and the Copper Canyon, where they retreated from Spanish colonists and miners. They are famous for running hundreds of miles in huarache sandals.
pop: speakers of the language according to the Mexican census; estimates vary widely
events: The first Jesuit mission.
The first of a series of Tarahumara revolts against the Spanish.

seri.text: A small nation of hunters and fishers on the coast of the Gulf of California and Tiburón Island, speaking a language with no known relatives. They never took up farming or mission life and survived repeated campaigns of extermination.
events: A Spanish punitive expedition to Tiburón Island.
Tiburón Island is recognized as Seri communal property.

shoshone.lifeway: hunter-gatherers; mounted bison hunters in the east
shoshone.text: A nation of the Great Basin and the Rocky Mountains. The Shoshone woman Sacagawea guided the Lewis and Clark expedition; Chief Washakie secured the Wind River Reservation for the Eastern Shoshone. The Comanche emerged from a southern branch of the Shoshone.
events: Sacagawea and the Lewis and Clark expedition.
The Bear River Massacre – about 250 Shoshone killed.
The Treaty of Fort Bridger creates the Wind River and Fort Hall reservations.

ute.lifeway: mountain hunter-gatherers; horsemen from the 17th century
ute.text: A mountain nation of the Rockies for whom the state of Utah is named. They were among the first to obtain horses from the Spanish; after gold and silver were discovered in Colorado they lost almost all their land.
events: A treaty recognizes the western third of Colorado as Ute land.
The Meeker incident and the White River War.
Most Utes are expelled from Colorado to Utah.

paiute.lifeway: hunter-gatherers of the high desert (pine nuts, fish, rabbits)
paiute.text: Hunter-gatherers of the arid Great Basin. In 1889 the Paiute prophet Wovoka founded the Ghost Dance movement, which spread among the Plains tribes; Sarah Winnemucca was the first Native American woman to publish a book in English.
pop: all Paiute (Northern and Southern) according to the census; approximate
events: The Pyramid Lake War.
Sarah Winnemucca publishes “Life Among the Piutes.”
Wovoka’s vision and the birth of the Ghost Dance.

nezperce.lifeway: salmon fishers, camas gatherers, and breeders of Appaloosa horses
nezperce.text: A nation of the Columbia Plateau, famous for horse breeding. In 1877 Chief Joseph led his people on a retreat of nearly 1,200 miles ahead of the army toward Canada; he surrendered 40 miles short of the border with the words “I will fight no more forever.”
events: The Nez Perce save the starving Lewis and Clark expedition.
The “Thief Treaty” shrinks the reservation by 90 percent.
The Nez Perce War and Chief Joseph’s retreat.

chumash.lifeway: maritime fishers and hunters; plank canoes (tomol) and shell-bead money
chumash.text: A seafaring nation of the Santa Barbara coast and the Channel Islands, with dense settlement, a complex society, and remarkable rock paintings. The Spanish mission system and introduced diseases reduced their numbers by more than 95 percent within a century.
events: Cabrillo sails through the Santa Barbara Channel.
Founding of the first of five missions on Chumash land.
The Chumash revolt at the missions.
terr: Santa Barbara coast and the Channel Islands

pomo.lifeway: acorn gatherers and fishers; master basket weavers
pomo.text: A group of related peoples of northern California (Clear Lake, Russian River) whose baskets are among the finest in the world. In 1850 the U.S. Army killed hundreds of Pomo on Bloody Island.
events: The Russians found Fort Ross on the Pomo coast.
The Bloody Island Massacre.
terr: Clear Lake and the Russian River

tlingit.lifeway: salmon fishers and sea hunters; totem poles, potlatch, clan houses
tlingit.text: A nation of the fjords and islands of southeastern Alaska with a rich carving tradition and matrilineal Raven and Eagle clans. In 1802 they captured the Russian fort at Sitka and never fully submitted to the Russians.
events: The Tlingit capture the Russian fort at Sitka.
Battle of Sitka – the Russians retake the fort.
The Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA).

haida.lifeway: seafarers in great cedar canoes; totem-pole carvers
haida.flag: Flag of Haida Gwaii (Council of the Haida Nation)
haida.text: The people of the Haida Gwaii archipelago, feared sea raiders and masters of carving in cedar and argillite. The smallpox epidemic of 1862 killed most of the nation. In 2024 British Columbia recognized Haida title to the entire archipelago.
events: First contact with the Spanish (Juan Pérez).
Smallpox epidemic.
Agreement recognizing Haida title to Haida Gwaii.
terr: Kaigani Haida (Prince of Wales Island, Alaska)

kwakwakawakw.lifeway: fishers and sea hunters; potlatch and ceremonial masks
kwakwakawakw.text: The peoples of northern Vancouver Island and the adjacent mainland, known for their spectacular potlatch ceremonies and transformation masks. Canada banned the potlatch from 1885 to 1951 and confiscated ceremonial objects.
events: Encounter with George Vancouver’s expedition.
The potlatch ban.
The raid on Dan Cranmer’s potlatch – masks and regalia are confiscated.
terr: Northern Vancouver Island and the adjacent coast

coastsalish.lifeway: salmon fishers, weavers, and builders of plank houses
coastsalish.text: Dozens of related nations around the Salish Sea (Puget Sound, the Strait of Georgia). Vancouver, Victoria, and Seattle now stand on their land – Seattle bears the name of Chief Si'ahl of the Duwamish and Suquamish.
events: George Vancouver’s expedition charts Puget Sound.
Treaty of Point Elliott.
The Boldt Decision awards the tribes half of the salmon catch.

chinook.text: Trading peoples of the lower Columbia River; their trade pidgin (Chinook Jargon) became the lingua franca of the entire Northwest. The “fever” (malaria) epidemic of 1830–1833 killed about 90 percent of the population.
events: Lewis and Clark winter at the mouth of the Columbia.
Start of a devastating malaria epidemic.
The Tansy Point treaties – never ratified by Congress.

dene.lifeway: caribou hunters following the herds between the taiga and the tundra
dene.text: The largest of the Dene nations, caribou hunters of the forest–tundra edge west of Hudson Bay. In 1715 the Chipewyan woman Thanadelthur brokered peace with the Cree and opened trade with the Hudson’s Bay Company.
events: Thanadelthur brokers peace between the Cree and the Chipewyan.
Smallpox epidemic.
Treaty 8.
terr: Denendeh – between Hudson Bay and Great Slave Lake

innu.lifeway: hunters of caribou and fur-bearing animals
innu.text: Caribou hunters of eastern Quebec and Labrador (Nitassinan), called Montagnais and Naskapi in older sources. They were among the first allies of the French – in 1603 they welcomed an alliance with Samuel de Champlain at Tadoussac.
events: Alliance with the French at Tadoussac.
The Labrador Innu are resettled at Davis Inlet.

gwichin.endonym: Dinjii Zhuh / Gwich'in (“people of a place”)
gwichin.lifeway: hunters of the Porcupine caribou herd
gwichin.text: The northernmost American Indian nation, living above the Arctic Circle from the Yukon River to the Mackenzie Delta. Their life is bound to the Porcupine caribou herd, whose calving grounds on the Alaska coast they have long defended against oil drilling.
pop: according to censuses in Canada and Alaska; the Gwich'in Council cites about 9,000
events: The Hudson’s Bay Company founds Fort Yukon.
The Gwich'in Comprehensive Land Claim Agreement in Canada.

beothuk.lifeway: hunters of caribou and seals; they painted their bodies and tools with red ocher
beothuk.flag: The nation died out in 1829 – it had no flag.
beothuk.text: The original inhabitants of Newfoundland, who painted their bodies with red ocher – possibly the origin of the term “Red Indians.” European fishermen cut them off from the coast; hunger, tuberculosis, and violence led to their extinction. The last known Beothuk, Shanawdithit, died in 1829.
pop: death of Shanawdithit, the last known Beothuk
events: John Cabot reaches Newfoundland.
Capture of Demasduit.
Shanawdithit dies.

inuit.countries: Canada (Nunavut, Nunavik, Nunatsiavut, Northwest Territories), U.S. (Alaska), Greenland
inuit.lifeway: hunters of sea mammals and caribou; igloos, kayaks, dog sleds
inuit.flag: Flag of the Canadian territory of Nunavut (1999), with an Inuit inuksuk
inuit.text: The people of the Arctic from Alaska to Greenland, descendants of the Thule culture, which spread east from Alaska around 1000–1200. They are not “Indians” but a distinct Indigenous group. In 1999 the territory of Nunavut (“our land”) was created in Canada.
pop: Canada (70,540) and U.S. (17,067); about 155,000 including Greenland
events: The Thule ancestors of the Inuit spread east from Alaska.
Encounter with Martin Frobisher’s expedition.
Families are forcibly relocated to the High Arctic.
The territory of Nunavut is created.
terr: Thule ancestors of the Inuit (northern Alaska)

aleut.text: Sea hunters of the Aleutian Islands. After 1741 Russian fur traders forced them to hunt sea otters; violence and disease cut their numbers by more than 80 percent. During World War II the Aleuts were forcibly evacuated and interned.
events: Bering’s expedition – the start of the Russian fur trade.
The Aleut revolt in the Fox Islands.
Japanese occupation of Attu and the forced evacuation of the Aleuts.

yupik.lifeway: salmon fishers and hunters of seals and walrus
yupik.text: Relatives of the Inuit in southwestern Alaska (the Yukon–Kuskokwim Delta) and Russian Chukotka. Central Alaskan Yup'ik is the most widely spoken Native language in Alaska today.
events: The Russians found the trading post of St. Michael.
ANCSA creates the Alaska Native regional corporations.

aztec.lifeway: urban civilization; farming on artificial islands (chinampas)
aztec.flag: The Aztec Empire had no flag in the modern sense; the eagle on a cactus on the Mexican flag comes from the legend of the founding of Tenochtitlan.
aztec.text: The Mexica of the island city of Tenochtitlan, allied with the cities of Texcoco and Tlacopan, built an empire that by 1519 controlled most of central Mexico. Hernán Cortés conquered it in 1521 with tens of thousands of Native allies. Their descendants, the Nahua, are the most numerous Indigenous people of Mexico today.
pop: estimated population of the empire (5–6 million); Tenochtitlan had about 200,000
events: Founding of Tenochtitlan.
The Triple Alliance is formed – the beginning of the empire.
Cortés enters Tenochtitlan.
Fall of Tenochtitlan.

maya.text: A civilization of city-states with its own writing and astronomy, whose Classic period peaked between 250 and 900. The Maya never disappeared: the last independent kingdom, Nojpetén, fell only in 1697, and millions of Maya live today in Yucatán, Chiapas, and Guatemala.
events: The Spanish conquer the Guatemalan highlands.
Fall of Nojpetén, the last Maya kingdom.
The Caste War of Yucatán (until 1901).
The Zapatista uprising in Chiapas.

purepecha.lifeway: farmers and fishers on Lake Pátzcuaro; metalworkers
purepecha.text: The Tarascan Empire, with its capital at Tzintzuntzan, was the only state the Aztecs never defeated – thanks in part to its bronze weapons. It submitted to the Spanish in 1530 without a major war.
pop: estimated population of the empire (0.75–1.5 million)
events: A crushing defeat of the Aztec army.
The Spanish execute the last ruler (cazonci), Tangaxuan II.

zapotec.lifeway: farmers; the urban civilization of Monte Albán
zapotec.text: One of the oldest civilizations of Mesoamerica – their capital Monte Albán was founded around 500 BC, and Zapotec writing is among the earliest in the Americas. Mexican president Benito Juárez was Zapotec.
events: Submission to the Spanish.
The Zapotec Benito Juárez becomes president of Mexico.
terr: Valley of Oaxaca and the Isthmus of Tehuantepec

mixtec.lifeway: farmers; renowned goldsmiths and codex painters
mixtec.text: The “People of the Rain” of mountainous western Oaxaca, divided into many small kingdoms. Mixtec pictorial codices record the genealogies of rulers back to the 10th century, among them the famous conqueror Eight Deer “Jaguar Claw.”
events: Birth of the ruler Eight Deer, who united the Mixtec.
Spanish conquest.

otomi.text: Among the oldest inhabitants of the central Mexican highlands, settled there long before the arrival of the Aztecs, to whom they later paid tribute. After 1521 they took part in settling the north as allies of the Spanish.
events: The Otomi leader Conín founds Querétaro.

totonac.text: The people of the Gulf coast, builders of the city of El Tajín and the first to cultivate vanilla. At Cempoala in 1519 they were the first to ally with Cortés against the Aztecs. They still perform the ceremony of the “flying men” (voladores).
events: The ruler of Cempoala allies with Cortés.

huichol.lifeway: mountain farmers; peyote pilgrimages, yarn paintings, and beadwork
huichol.text: A mountain nation of the Sierra Madre Occidental whose isolation helped it preserve its pre-Christian religion. Each year they walk hundreds of miles to the desert of Wirikuta to gather the sacred peyote cactus.
events: The Spanish subdue neighboring Nayarit; the Huichol keep de facto autonomy.

mississippian.lifeway: corn farmers; towns with platform mounds, ruled by chiefs
mississippian.flag: An archaeological culture – it had no flag.
mississippian.text: The largest pre-Columbian civilization north of Mexico. Its center, Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, had more inhabitants around 1100 than London did at the time, and Monks Mound is taller than a ten-story building. The heirs of this culture are the Muscogee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Natchez, and other nations of the Southeast.
events: Beginnings of the culture as corn farming spreads.
Cahokia’s explosive growth (the “Big Bang”).
Cahokia is abandoned.
De Soto’s expedition meets the last great chiefdoms; epidemics then shatter them.
terr: Mississippi, Ohio, and Tennessee river basins

anasazi.lifeway: farmers; stone “great houses” and cliff dwellings
anasazi.flag: An archaeological culture – it had no flag.
anasazi.text: Builders of the great stone houses of Chaco Canyon and the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde. After the great drought at the end of the 13th century they left the Four Corners region and moved to the Rio Grande and the Hopi mesas – today’s Pueblo peoples, Hopi, and Zuni are their descendants. The older name Anasazi comes from Navajo and is rejected by Pueblo people.
pop: rough estimate for the Mesa Verde region alone
events: Construction of the great houses of Chaco Canyon begins (Pueblo Bonito).
Chaco declines after a long drought.
The cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde (Cliff Palace).
Start of the “Great Drought” (until 1299) and the departure from the Four Corners.

hohokam.lifeway: desert farmers with a vast network of irrigation canals
hohokam.flag: An archaeological culture – it had no flag.
hohokam.text: Farmers of the Salt and Gila river valleys who built hundreds of miles of irrigation canals – the largest in pre-Columbian North America; some of Phoenix’s modern canals follow their routes. The O'odham (Tohono O'odham and Akimel O'odham) are considered their descendants.
events: Peak of the canal network and the ball courts.
Construction of the “Great House” at Casa Grande.
The culture collapses after floods and drought.

toltec.flag: A pre-Columbian civilization – it had no flag.
toltec.text: A civilization whose capital, Tula, is famous for its warrior columns (the “Atlanteans”). The Aztecs revered the Toltecs as their cultural ancestors, and the word “toltecatl” meant a master craftsman to them. Historians dispute the real extent of Toltec power.
pop: estimate for the city of Tula (30,000–60,000)
events: The rise of Tula.
Tula is burned and abandoned.

dorset.lifeway: hunters of seals and walrus on the sea ice; no bows or dog sleds
dorset.flag: An archaeological culture – it had no flag.
dorset.text: The people of the eastern Arctic before the arrival of the Inuit. Inuit legends describe them as the Tuniit – strong but shy giants. Between 1200 and 1500 they were replaced by the Thule ancestors of the Inuit arriving from Alaska; genetic studies show the two groups hardly mixed.
events: The culture emerges.
Possible encounters with the Norse (the “Skrælings” of the sagas).
It disappears from most of its territory after the arrival of the Thule.
